title: Cyclic decomposition over the perfect-field Frobenius skew-polynomial ring
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] of characteristic $p>0$, and put $\sigma(c)=c^p$. Define $A=k_\sigma[F]$ to be the ring of finite sums $\sum_i c_iF^i$, with coefficientwise addition and multiplication $(cF^i)(bF^j)=c\,b^{p^i}F^{i+j}$. Assume that every element of $k$ is a $p$-th power. For every finitely generated left $A$-module $M$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], there are an integer $q\geq0$, elements $g_1,\ldots,g_q\in A$, and a left $A$-module isomorphism $$M\simeq\bigoplus_{i=1}^q A/Ag_i.$$ Here $Ag_i=\{ag_i:a\in A\}$ is the principal left ideal, the quotient is a quotient of left modules (not asserted to be a quotient ring), $g_i=0$ is allowed, and $\bigoplus$ is the finite module direct sum. No irreducibility condition on the $g_i$ is imposed.

source.place: Proposition 14.51, printed p.297, in the cyclic-decomposition form actually used in the proof of Proposition 14.52; left and right division algorithms on printed p.296. Source correction: omit the erroneous words "or irreducible" in the printed Proposition 14.51.

proof.text: The map $\sigma(c)=c^p$ is an automorphism: in characteristic $p$, the binomial formula gives $(a+b)^p=a^p+b^p$, and multiplication and $1$ are preserved. If $a^p=b^p$, then $(a-b)^p=0$ in the field, so $a=b$. Surjectivity is the perfectness hypothesis. Thus the ring in the statement is the automorphism skew ring of the division lemma.

source.place: Printed p.296, last paragraph: perfectness makes Frobenius an automorphism.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-skew-polynomial-two-sided-division]. Every nonzero left ideal $I$ is principal: choose $g\in I\setminus\{0\}$ of least degree. For $f\in I$ write $f=qg+r$; then $r=f-qg\in I$, so minimality forces $r=0$. Hence $I=Ag$. The zero left ideal is $A0$. Retain both division algorithms with $\delta(g)=\deg g$ for the matrix reduction below.

source.place: Printed p.296, division algorithms and the left-ideal assertion of Proposition 14.50.

proof.text: Choose generators $m_1,\ldots,m_n$ of $M$ and define $\pi:A^n\to M$ by $\pi(x)=\sum_i x_i m_i$, using row coordinates for the left free module. It is left linear and surjective. By [lem-sfb-left-principal-finite-submodules], $K=\ker\pi$ has finitely many generators $v_1,\ldots,v_m$; use them as the rows of a matrix $C$. Then $K=\{xC:x\in A^m\}$. The map $[x]\mapsto\pi(x)$ identifies $A^n/K$ with $M$: it is well defined, surjective, and injective because $\pi(x)=0$ exactly when $x\in K$.

source.place: Proposition 14.51, finite-generator presentation underlying the comparison with the polynomial-ring proof; finite relations follow from Proposition 14.50.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-two-sided-division-matrix-diagonalization] with the degree function and the two division algorithms from [lem-sfb-skew-polynomial-two-sided-division], obtaining $D=UCV$. For row coordinates, $x\mapsto xV$ is left $A$-linear and invertible. Since $\{xU:x\in A^m\}=A^m$, one has $\{xD\}=\{xCV\}=KV$. Therefore this map induces $A^n/K\simeq A^n/\{xD\}$. This verifies the side of every multiplication without commuting coefficients.

source.place: Proposition 14.51, matrix reduction in the polynomial-ring comparison, with the left-module convention made explicit.

proof.text: For $1\leq i\leq n$ put $g_i=D_{ii}$ if $i\leq\min(m,n)$ and $g_i=0$ otherwise. The rows of $D$ generate precisely the vectors $x\in A^n$ with $x_i\in Ag_i$ for every $i$. Consequently $[x]\mapsto([x_1],\ldots,[x_n])$ is a left-linear bijection from $A^n/\{xD\}$ to $\bigoplus_{i=1}^n A/Ag_i$: its kernel is exactly the displayed relation module and representatives of each finite tuple give surjectivity. Composing the explicit bijections yields the assertion with $q=n$. If $n=0$, $M=0$ and the direct sum is empty; zero diagonal entries yield the allowed free cyclic factors.

source.place: Proposition 14.51 corrected cyclic-decomposition conclusion; the exact version used in Proposition 14.52.
